prompt: Which kind of RNA transports amino acids to the ribosomes?

choices.why: mRNA carries genetic messages from DNA to the ribosomes.
rRNA, complexed with protein, makes up the ribosomes themselves.
Small RNAs do jobs such as silencing transcription and modifying other RNAs.

explanation: mRNA carries genetic messages from DNA to ribosomes; rRNA complexed with protein provides the physical makeup of the ribosomes; tRNA transports amino acids to the ribosomes, where they are joined to make proteins.

prompt: Uracil forms strong hydrogen bonds to adenine, as thymine does in DNA. How many hydrogen bonds hold a U–A base pair together?
explanation: In Exercise 28.4.1, uracil and adenine form two hydrogen bonds, each base acting as a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor. This matches the two hydrogen bonds of the A–T pair in DNA.

prompt: In bacteria, where is the promoter sequence that RNA polymerase binds to?

choices.text: Upstream (5′) of the transcription start site
Downstream (3′) of the transcription start site
choices.why: The promoter lies upstream, on the 5′ side of the start site.

choices.text: At the very end of the gene, where transcription stops
choices.why: The promoter marks where transcription begins, upstream of the start site.

choices.text: On the mRNA, at its 5′ end
choices.why: The promoter is a DNA sequence that RNA polymerase recognizes before any mRNA is made.

explanation: Transcription begins when RNA polymerase recognizes and binds to a promoter sequence on DNA, typically about 40 base pairs located upstream (5′) of the transcription start site. Within it are two hexameric consensus sequences, 10 and 35 base pairs upstream of the start.

prompt: During transcription, about how many base pairs of the growing RNA remain hydrogen-bonded to the DNA template at any one time?
explanation: Several turns of DNA untwist, exposing 14 or so base pairs. Ribonucleotides line up on the template and bond 5′ → 3′, and at any one time about 12 base pairs of the growing RNA remain hydrogen-bonded to the DNA template.

prompt: Which DNA strand is transcribed to give RNA?

choices.why: The sense strand contains the gene, but it is the antisense strand that serves as the template. The RNA ends up as a copy of the sense strand.
Unlike replication, only one of the two DNA strands is transcribed.

choices.text: A ribosomal RNA strand bound to the DNA
choices.why: Transcription uses a DNA strand as its template. rRNA, complexed with protein, makes up the ribosomes.

explanation: Only one DNA strand is transcribed. The strand that contains the gene is the sense, or coding, strand; the strand that gets transcribed is the antisense, or noncoding, strand. Because the RNA is complementary to the antisense strand, it is a copy of the sense strand with U in place of T.

prompt: The DNA sense (coding) strand of a short gene reads 5′-ATGCCT-3′. What is the mRNA sequence, written 5′→3′?

choices.why: This is the complement of the sense strand. The mRNA is complementary to the antisense strand, so it copies the sense strand.
This pairs each base with its partner but doesn't reverse the order. Besides, mRNA copies the sense strand rather than pairing with it.
RNA contains U, not T. The mRNA has U wherever the sense strand has T.

explanation: The RNA made in transcription is a copy of the DNA sense strand: the complement of the complement is the original. The only difference is that RNA has U everywhere the sense strand has T, so 5′-ATGCCT-3′ gives 5′-AUGCCU-3′.

prompt: What RNA sequence, written 5′→3′, is complementary to the DNA sequence 5′-GATTACCGTA-3′?

choices.why: These are the right partner bases in 3′→5′ order: the book writes them (3′) CUAAUGGCAU (5′). Read from the 5′ end they give UACGGUAAUC.
RNA uses U, not T. Adenine in DNA pairs with uracil in RNA.
This copies the DNA with U for T instead of pairing each base with its complement.

explanation: Pair G with C, A with U, T with A, and C with G. The complement of (5′) GATTACCGTA (3′) is (3′) CUAAUGGCAU (5′), as in Exercise 28.4.2. Written 5′→3′, it is (5′) UACGGUAAUC (3′).

prompt: From what DNA sequence, written 5′→3′, was the RNA sequence 5′-UUCGCAGAGU-3′ transcribed?

choices.why: These are the right partner bases, but in 3′→5′ order. Read from the 5′ end they give ACTCTGCGAA.
This is the sense strand, which the RNA copies. The transcribed (antisense) strand is its complement.
DNA contains T, not U.

explanation: The transcribed DNA strand is complementary to the RNA: U pairs with A, A with T, C with G, and G with C. The complement of (5′) UUCGCAGAGU (3′), written 5′→3′, is (5′) ACTCTGCGAA (3′), as in Exercise 28.4.3.

prompt: The maize gene for triose phosphate isomerase has eight noncoding introns that account for about 70% of its DNA base pairs. What percentage of its base pairs are in the coding exons?
explanation: The nine coding exons account for only about 30% of the base pairs (100% − 70% = 30%). The introns are cut out of the transcribed mRNA, and the exons are joined by spliceosome enzymes.

prompt: In vertebrates and flowering plants, what happens to the introns in a gene?

choices.text: They are noncoding sections that are cut out of the transcribed mRNA
They are coding sections that are joined together by spliceosome enzymes
choices.why: Those are the exons. Introns are the noncoding sections that get cut out.

choices.text: They are promoter sequences where RNA polymerase binds
choices.why: The promoter lies upstream of the start site. Introns interrupt the gene itself.

choices.text: They are never transcribed into mRNA
choices.why: Introns are transcribed. They are cut out of the mRNA afterward.

explanation: A gene often begins in a section called an exon, is interrupted by a noncoding section called an intron, and resumes in another exon. The final mRNA results only after the noncoded sections are cut out of the transcribed mRNA and the remaining pieces are joined by spliceosome enzymes.
